messages.content:
Title: Diagnosis
Details:
The failing test `testCalendarTimezoneRespected` checks that the timezone printed by `FastDateFormat` when formatting a `Calendar` instance respects the timezone set on the Calendar itself.

The failure and issue report state that FastDateFormat's handling of the "z" pattern (timezone name) does not respect the timezone of the Calendar passed to it. Instead, it always prints the timezone of the machine's default timezone, ignoring the timezone set on the Calendar, although the actual time respects the calendar's timezone.

Diagnosis and Analysis:
- Looking at the test: A `Calendar` is created with a different timezone than the system default. Both `SimpleDateFormat` and the tested `FastDateFormat` format the calendar. The test expects matching strings, specifically checking that the timezone name matches and respects the calendar's timezone.
- `FastDateFormat.format(Calendar)` calls `FastDatePrinter.format(Calendar)`, which then uses internal rules to format the calendar.
- The mismatch implies that the timezone used to format the timezone pattern "z" is not taken from the Calendar but from somewhere else.
- `FastDateFormat.getInstance(pattern)` is called without specifying a timezone, which internally calls cache.getInstance with null timezone - which defaults to the system default timezone.
- So, the formatter instance `FastDateFormat` is created with the system default timezone at creation.
- Because the instance has a fixed cached timezone (default system timezone), it does not dynamically honor the timezone of the Calendar passed at formatting time.
- The formatting rules applied by FastDatePrinter use the cached timezone from the formatter instance rather than the Calendar's timezone.
- This explains the test result: although the Calendar's time respects its own timezone, the "z" pattern always prints the default timezone name.

Recent bug reports are unrelated.

In summary, the root cause is that FastDateFormat caches the timezone at the instance level (set at creation) and does not dynamically adapt to the timezone of the calendar passed to its format() methods. Thus, the "z" pattern is formatted with an incorrect fixed timezone.

This issue was introduced in recent work aiming to support parsing and caching, which inadvertently fixed the timezone to the instance rather than using calendar's runtime timezone.

Hence, the failure originates from the fact that FastDateFormat does not delegate the timezone for the "z" pattern dynamically from the Calendar argument, and instead uses the instance-created timezone.

---

Next, I will suggest which methods would be the best to be fixed.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
